strengths: Novel and well-motivated integration of proprioception and multi-contact tactile signals as explicit geometric constraints within a flow-matching 3D generative pipeline, addressing a real gap: prior occlusion-aware 3D reconstruction (e.g., Amodal3R) relies on vision-only conditioning and cannot resolve ambiguity from severe hand occlusion.

Technically coherent design: a Structure-VAE over pose-aware, camera-aligned metric SDF grids enables the same physics losses (contact-consistency, non-interpenetration) to be used both as training objectives and as decoder-based guidance at inference, with sensible stabilization details (time-weighted physics terms, saturation function, trust region, EMA guidance).

The shared 3D grid with the posed end-effector elegantly yields implicit pose estimation and metric scale, and the pipeline integrates naturally with TRELLIS/SLat and Sam3D-style refinement for textured output.

Reasonably thorough experimental evidence: occlusion-stratified evaluation on YCB (22,680 test images), sensing ablations showing clear gains from proprioception and touch, tactile-noise robustness analysis tied to grid discretization, pose estimation results, and real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an end-effector unseen in training (cross-embodiment transfer).
Honest limitations section (calibration sensitivity, fixed 64^3 resolution in a shared grid, limited generalization guarantees), and extensive supplementary material improving reproducibility.

The paper covers both aspects convincingly: simulation + real robot experiments demonstrate feasibility of the approach, and the methodological contributions (physics losses + inference guidance + pose-aware SDF conditioning) are substantive enough for an algorithms contribution. The two facets reinforce each other.
weaknesses: The central physics claim is not quantitatively verified: despite non-interpenetration and contact-consistency being the headline contribution, no metric of physical plausibility (e.g., interpenetration volume/depth, contact alignment error, on-grid feasibility violations) is reported for any method. The reader cannot verify that the physics guidance actually reduces interpenetration in aggregate — only a single qualitative trajectory (Fig. A3) is shown. A table of physical-violation statistics across occlusion bins and an ablation of inference-time guidance (guidance strength η, decay β, guidance on/off) are needed.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline are mixed: SAM3D (vision-only, larger capacity/data) beats the proposed method on CD in B1–B4 and on F@0.02 and EMD in the real-world setting; the proposed method wins mainly on NC and Voxel IoU. The paper's own text acknowledges vision-only models can match or exceed its reconstruction quality at low occlusion. The advantage should be framed and verified more carefully (e.g., variance/significance over grasps, per-object breakdown), and the dataset-size/capacity disparity between the proposed model and SAM3D complicates attribution of improvements to the physical signals.

Comparison protocol for pose estimation is asymmetric: SAM3D is evaluated in a best-case configuration using ground-truth depth, and only against SAM3D. Additional baselines or at least a no-guidance variant would strengthen the claim that touch/proprioception (rather than architecture or data) drive the improvements; the sensing ablation partially covers this but only for reconstruction.

Real-world evaluation is narrow: five YCB objects, subset of grasps, and only reconstruction metrics (no pose or physical-plausibility metrics on the real robot), even though calibration noise is identified as a key failure mode. Qualitative evidence (Fig. 4, Fig. A2) suggests non-trivial hand–object misalignment artifacts.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: Table 1 contains a likely typo (Sam3D B3 NC = 0.081 vs. 0.803 in other bins), 'Normal consistencty'/'Unione' typos, Eq. (1) contains a malformed symbol (Rv), and hyperparameters (λ_NI, λ_C, α, σ_min, training schedule) are deferred without sufficient detail in the main text. No statement about code or model release is given, which is important for reproducibility of a system this complex.

Fairness of the comparison: the proposed model is trained on a smaller dataset and reduced capacity than both baselines, which cuts both ways — it makes the gains impressive but also makes it unclear whether the full method with matched capacity would dominate, or whether observed wins would vanish.

strengths: Original and well-motivated idea: integrating proprioception and multi-contact tactile signals as explicit 3D conditioning for occlusion-aware generative reconstruction, going beyond prior vision-only occlusion methods (Amodal3R) and vision+touch mapping works.

The physics objectives (non-interpenetration and contact-consistency losses) are used coherently in both finetuning and inference-time decoder guidance, and the method description is generally clear and reproducible in its mathematical detail (Eqs. 2-17).

Reasonable experimental design: stratification by occlusion level, sensing ablations (vision-only, no-touch), tactile noise robustness study, and cross-embodiment transfer to a real humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector — a genuine and valuable demonstration for an Applied/Systems contribution.
A candid Limitations section that correctly identifies dependence on calibration/masks, fixed 64^3 resolution, and embodiment generalization as open issues.
weaknesses: The central claim — that the method yields physically plausible reconstructions — is never directly quantified. There is no interpenetration volume, contact-error, or physical-feasibility metric anywhere in the paper; the 'physically grounded' contribution is evaluated only through generic shape metrics (CD, NC, F-score, IoU, EMD), leaving the key novelty claim unsupported by dedicated evidence.

The quantitative advantage over the strongest baseline (SAM3D) is mixed and partially overstated: in Table 1, SAM3D wins F@0.02 in bins B1-B4 (e.g., 0.265 vs 0.215 in B1), yet the text claims improvement on all metrics 'except in the least-occluded regime', which contradicts the table. In the real-world setting (Table 3), the method again loses on F@0.02 (0.186 vs 0.225). The improvement case rests mainly on Voxel-IoU and NC.

Comparison fairness is questionable: baselines were trained on larger datasets and, for pose estimation, SAM3D is evaluated in a contrived best-case configuration with ground-truth depth, while the proposed method uses privileged proprioceptive state (joint encoders, calibrated extrinsics, forward kinematics) that is unavailable in purely vision-based settings. The sensing ablation helps, but gains from hand-pose conditioning conflate scale/pose anchoring with genuine shape completion improvements.

Evidence of insufficient polish undermines confidence: apparent typos in Table 1 (Sam3D NC in B3 reported as 0.081, likely 0.781), truncated/rounded values in Table 2 (ICP-Rot 'All: 10', ADD-S '0.11'/'0.19' with inconsistent precision), inconsistent bolding/formatting in Tables 2-3, and writing errors ('Normal consistencty', 'Intersection over Unione', 'Earth's Mover's Distance', broken equation rendering on page 6).

Real-world validation is thin: only five YCB objects, single-hand platform, no controlled study of the sim2real gap or end-effector transfer (acknowledged), and the method's slightly degraded real-world scores are explained post hoc by calibration noise without direct analysis.
No statement about code, data, or model release, which limits reproducibility of a pipeline that depends on multiple custom components (Structure-VAE, grasp data generation, tactile conditioning).

Contribution type: while submitted as Algorithms/General, this is best viewed as Applied/Systems; under that lens the real-robot demonstration is valuable, but the system's dependence on accurate calibration, occlusion masks, and contact detection weakens its practical impact claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: amodal, metric-scale 3D reconstruction of objects under severe hand occlusion, where vision alone is fundamentally underconstrained. Framing this as a physically grounded generative inference problem and integrating proprioception and multi-contact touch as explicit 3D geometric constraints is a novel and well-motivated contribution relative to prior occlusion-aware generative methods (e.g., Amodal3R) and vision-tactile fusion works.

The method is technically well-specified and reasonably sound: a pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation with a Structure-VAE, flow matching in latent space, contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses used both during finetuning and as decoder-based guidance at inference (Eqs. 15-17) is a coherent and reproducible design. The two-sensor role is well justified (touch provides positive surface constraints, the hand provides negative non-interpenetration constraints).

Experimental evidence is fairly comprehensive for this type of contribution: simulation evaluation stratified by occlusion level across multiple standard metrics, pose-estimation evaluation, sensing ablations (vision-only vs. no-touch vs. full), tactile-noise ablations tied to grid quantization, and a real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an end-effector unseen during training. This cross-embodiment transfer is a meaningful validation of the representation choice (shared 3D grid conditioning).

The limitations section is honest and substantive, correctly identifying dependence on calibration, fixed-resolution grid fidelity, and unresolved generalization across hand morphologies and tactile layouts.
The proposed Stage A output integrates naturally with existing two-stage shape-appearance pipelines (SLat/Sam3D), increasing practical impact and reproducibility potential.
weaknesses: The central claim is 'physically plausible reconstructions' (reduced interpenetration, surfaces aligned with contacts), yet the paper never quantifies physical plausibility. All reported metrics (CD, NC, F@0.02, Voxel-IoU, EMD, 3D IoU, ADD-S) measure geometric accuracy, not penetration volume, contact alignment error, or feasibility rate. There is also no ablation of inference-time physics guidance (guidance on vs. off), so the contribution of Eqs. 15-17 relative to finetuning-time losses alone is unverified. This is a substantive evidentiary gap for the paper's headline contribution.

In the real-world setting (Tab. 3), the method is actually worse than SAM3D on several metrics (F@0.02: 0.186 vs. 0.225; EMD: 0.190 vs. 0.185), and the gains over Amodal3R in the real setting largely mirror SAM3D's, weakening the case that touch/proprioception conditioning is decisive in real conditions. The explanation given (encoder/calibration noise) is plausible but anecdotal; a controlled degradation study would be needed to substantiate it.

Baseline fairness is questionable: SAM3D is trained on much larger data with greater model capacity and, for pose estimation, is given ground-truth depth to reach its 'best case'. Meanwhile the proposed model benefits from privileged simulation-side information (perfect forward kinematics, exact contact locations, GT masks in simulation). The comparison cannot isolate the effect of multimodal conditioning from data/model asymmetries.

Simulated grasps are generated by a learned grasp-synthesis model rather than a physics simulator, so contact distributions may not reflect real contact mechanics; the real-world transfer is limited to five YCB objects, a small evaluation set.

Presentation issues that should be fixed: an obvious typographical error in Table 1 (Sam3D B3 NC = 0.081, inconsistent with surrounding values ~0.77-0.84); 'Normal consistencty', 'Voxel Intersection over Unione', 'Earths' Mover's Distance'; Eq. 1 renders with an undefined '\Rv'; the 'canonical R,R,R 3D grid' formatting on p.5; and Stage B is described only briefly ('primarily an integration step') with no quantitative contribution of its own.

strengths: The problem addressed—metric-scale amodal 3D reconstruction under severe hand occlusion—is practically important for robotic manipulation, and the paper is the first (to the authors' knowledge and reasonably argued) to integrate proprioception and multi-contact touch as explicit geometric constraints inside a flow-matching 3D generative pipeline, rather than only using touch for local shape estimates or pose estimation.

The technical design is coherent and well-motivated: the pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF shared by hand and object enables both contact-consistency and non-interpenetration objectives as differentiable training losses and as decoder-guided sampling terms (Eqs. 12-17), and the two-channel contact representation (binary occupancy plus distance field) is a sensible design choice, validated by the component ablation (Table 4).

The experimental evidence is thorough for the contribution type: results stratified by occlusion level, comparisons against relevant baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D), sensing-modality ablations (Vision-Only vs No-Touch vs full), noise-robustness studies (tactile, mask, kinematic perturbations), and training/inference component ablations, which together credibly isolate the value of proprioception and touch and show physics losses matter far more than inference guidance.

The paper demonstrates sim-to-real transfer on a real humanoid robot with an end-effector unseen during training, plus an additional evaluation on the DexYCB human-hand benchmark (Table A1), showing competitive or better results than dedicated hand-object methods with ~30x faster inference and much higher reconstruction rate; the comparison caveats (R.R., metric differences) are honestly stated.

The limitations section is substantive and specific (calibration/kinematic sensitivity, 64^3 fixed resolution and shared-grid resolution loss, camera-aligned vs object-centric frame), and the supplementary material provides enough detail (data generation, sprite placement, grasp simulation, seed sensitivity) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core evaluation is almost entirely in simulation: training and quantitative testing use synthetic renders of grasp scenes, and real-world validation is limited to five YCB objects with aggregate metrics only; the claimed real-world applicability would be strengthened by more objects, more trials, and per-object breakdowns.

Gains over the strongest baseline (SAM3D) are mixed rather than uniform: the method loses on F@0.02 in the least-occluded bin and overall in simulation (0.189 vs 0.228) and on the real-world F@0.02 (0.186 vs 0.225), winning mainly on CD, NC, Voxel-IoU, and EMD; the paper should more carefully quantify the trade-off between geometric fidelity and thresholded surface metrics, especially since thin-structure fidelity is admitted to suffer at 64^3 resolution.

Pose-estimation claims rest on a comparison where SAM3D is given ground-truth depth point maps; while the rationale is explained, a fairer operating-point analysis (e.g., SAM3D with estimated depth, or a dedicated 6D pose baseline) would make the advantage more convincing.

Physical plausibility—the paper's central claim—is not reported as a metric in the main simulation/real-world tables; interpenetration and contact-consistency errors appear only in the DexYCB table (I.V.) and anecdotally. Direct quantitative reporting of non-interpenetration and contact alignment under the main protocol would substantiate the headline claim.

Tactile input is simulated by thresholding contact events, and real-world touch comes from thresholded taxel activations on fingertip sensors only; the sensitivity of results to contact detection errors, contact coverage (no palm/dorsal sensing), and the sim-to-real tactile gap is not systematically characterized beyond additive spatial noise.

Presentation issues reduce polish: several formula typos and rendering artifacts (e.g., Eqs. 2, 5, 6 show misplaced symbols such as 'S(x)' for sigma, 'Smax' artifacts), a corrupted value in Table 1 (Sam3D B3 NC listed as 0.081), and grammatical errors in the supplementary ('tryue', 'It perform substantially worse', incomplete sentence before 'we tested multiple seeds'). These do not undermine the science but should be corrected.

Some choices lack justification in the main text, e.g., the loss weights (lambda_NI, lambda_C, lambda_L1, etc.), the guidance hyperparameters (beta, eta), and the number of sampling steps; their absence limits reproducibility from the main paper alone, and no variance/significance reporting accompanies the main tables (seed averaging is only mentioned in the supplement).

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and relatively unexplored: using proprioceptive hand geometry and multi-contact tactile signals as explicit geometric constraints (conditioning, training losses, and inference-time guidance) for amodal 3D generative reconstruction under severe occlusion. This is a genuine gap relative to vision-only occlusion-aware methods like Amodal3R and SAM3D.

The technical design is coherent: a pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation in a shared hand–object grid enables gradient-based contact-consistency and non-interpenetration objectives, used both as finetuning losses and as decoder-guided sampling control. The time-weighted physics losses and EMA-based guidance term are sensible engineering choices.

The sensing ablation (Table 4) provides the strongest evidence for the paper's claim: Vision-Only (CD 0.142, Voxel IoU 0.357) vs. full model (CD 0.033, Voxel IoU 0.586) shows large, consistent gains from proprioception and touch, and the component ablations (physics losses, contact representations) are informative.

The paper evaluates both in simulation (22,680 test images across occlusion strata, multiple standard metrics) and on a real humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector, including a DexYCB comparison against hand–object reconstruction baselines (Table A1), and includes an honest limitations and noise-robustness analysis that explains the real-world performance drop.
Adequate attribution of data and methods; the paper is transparent about building on TRELLIS [75], Amodal3R [73], and guidance heuristics from [68].
weaknesses: Despite 'physically grounded' being the central claim, the main experiments never directly quantify physical plausibility. Tables 1–3 report only geometry metrics (CD, NC, F@0.02, Voxel IoU, EMD); no interpenetration volume or contact-consistency error is reported for simulation or the real robot (I.V. appears only in the DexYCB supplement). The paper's headline contribution is therefore only indirectly supported.

The quantitative wins over the strongest baseline (SAM3D) are mixed rather than clear-cut: in Table 1, SAM3D beats the proposed method on CD and F@0.02 in B1 and on F@0.02 overall (0.228 vs. 0.189); in the real world (Table 3) SAM3D still wins on F@0.02 (0.225 vs. 0.186) and EMD. The improvement narrative relies mainly on NC and Voxel IoU, which deserves more careful discussion than it receives.

The contribution is largely a composition of existing components: TRELLIS-style structured latents, Amodal3R-style occlusion conditioning, a standard VAE + flow-matching recipe, and generic physics losses. Individually, the pieces are straightforward; the novelty rests on the multimodal conditioning scheme and its integration, which is valuable but incremental from an algorithms standpoint.

Presentation quality is below bar for submission: Table 2 contains obvious errors (ICP-Rot reported as '10', ADD-S as '0.07', ADD-S@0.1 as '0.73'); Table 1 shows Sam3D B3 NC = 0.081 (clearly a typo, inconsistent with neighboring values); the supplementary contains unfinished text and typos ('it's tryue', an orphaned 'we tested...' sentence, 'Iergba'). These errors in key results tables undermine confidence in the experimental bookkeeping.

Real-world validation is narrow: only 5 YCB objects, a single platform, no end-effector-identity control (acknowledged in Supp. B.1), and the method underperforms a vision-only baseline on several metrics in that setting. The cross-embodiment transfer claim is thus only weakly evidenced.

Baseline fairness is uneven: both baselines are trained on larger datasets and SAM3D has a larger model; there is no comparison against a retrained vision-only variant at matched data/model scale (the Vision-Only ablation differs in conditioning and mask distribution, as the authors themselves note), so the attribution of gains to touch/proprioception versus training differences is not fully isolated.

Dependence on accurate hand–eye calibration, forward kinematics, and masks is a substantial practical constraint for a robotics-facing method, and the paper shows (Fig. A2) that calibration errors visibly degrade results; the mitigation offered (guidance partially correcting errors) is anecdotal rather than quantified.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: integrating proprioception (posed hand geometry) and multi-contact tactile signals as 3D conditioning into a flow-matching generative reconstruction pipeline, addressing a real gap where amodal completion methods rely on vision alone.

Sound technical design: the pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation enables differentiable physics constraints (contact-consistency and non-interpenetration) used both as training losses and as decoder-based guidance during sampling, providing a coherent story for 'physically grounded generative inference'.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: reconstruction and pose metrics stratified by occlusion level (Tab. 1-2), real-world deployment on a humanoid with a different end-effector (Tab. 3), an unusually thorough ablation covering sensing modalities, input noise (masks, kinematics, tactile), physics losses, guidance, and contact representations (Tab. 4), plus a comparison on DexYCB against human-hand baselines (Tab. A1) with honest discussion of evaluation-protocol differences.

Strong ablation signal: the sensing ablation clearly attributes gains to proprioception and touch (Vision-Only CD 0.142 vs. full 0.033), and the physics-loss ablation shows substantial drops when removed, substantiating the core claims.
Candid limitations section covering calibration dependence, fixed 64³ grid resolution, and the shared-grid tradeoff; honest reporting of real-world degradation and seed sensitivity in the supplement.
weaknesses: Inconsistency between text and Table 1: the paper claims improvement over SAM3D 'on all metrics, except in the least-occluded regime for F@0.02', but F@0.02 is actually lower than SAM3D in bins B1-B3 AND on the full set (0.189 vs. 0.228); only CD, NC, Voxel-IoU, and EMD are better. This overstatement must be corrected.

Real-world gains are modest and mixed: in Tab. 3 our method leads on CD, NC, and Voxel-IoU but trails SAM3D on F@0.02 (0.186 vs. 0.225) and EMD; SAM3D also uses ground-truth-depth point maps in the pose comparison, making the pose-estimation advantage partly a comparison-protocol artifact. Real-world evaluation covers only five YCB objects with no statistical analysis.

Dependence on privileged inputs weakens practicality: the method requires accurate occluder/visibility masks, calibrated camera-hand extrinsics, and reliable tactile contact localization, and the noise ablation itself shows kinematic noise is the dominant failure mode; no automatic mask/pose estimation pipeline is demonstrated end-to-end.

Limited baseline breadth: only Amodal3R and SAM3D in the main results; human-hand baselines are deferred to the supplement and run under non-comparable protocols (different metrics, reconstruction-rate filtering, much slower inference), so the claimed comparability there is soft.

Inference-time physics guidance yields only marginal improvement (Tab. 4: 0.036 vs. 0.033 CD), meaning the headline 'physics guidance during sampling' contribution contributes little empirically; the paper states this honestly but the framing somewhat overweights it.

Fixed camera-aligned 64³ shared grid limits geometric fidelity and ties the method to a single viewpoint; the authors acknowledge an object-centric alternative, but the chosen design has unexplored consequences for multi-view or dynamic scenes.

Writing and presentation issues that need cleanup: Table 1 contains an apparent typo (Sam3D B3 NC = 0.081, likely 0.781); the supplement contains unfinished sentences/typos ('we tested multiple seeds...' fragment, "it's tryue"), and Eq. (1) notation (R_g, t introduced before definition) is slightly loose.
